strength: It goes all in on what the pilot says works: controllers, sent within 60 days of a pricing-page change, no links, the 9-to-4 proof written as a sentence, and an honest 6.8% to 7.9% reply target that doesn't multiply untested gains.

strength: A complete, runnable playbook: the right segment, trigger-first send order with a fallback opener for unflagged contacts, an opt-out footer, suppression rules, and pilot-based expectations with the arithmetic shown.

strength: It nails our three signals in the post itself. The title says Asia-Pacific hours and gives local times. The weekend rotation gets its own section that admits past hires found it unclear. Writing is weighted 50% with a realistic, stressed customer email to answer.

strength: It turns the raw table into 'agencies are 27% of trials but 60% of Semrush losses' and shows the arithmetic, so the whole case rests on our own numbers.

strength: It gives a clean win/lose table and an honest positioning call: own the trusted data inside the agency's Monday report, and skip PPC parity this year. Every target is concrete, with checked maths and a sample-size check on the free-account test.

strength: It turns the migration problem into hard launch gates: zero lost hotkeys across 1,000 real beta setups, a one-step undo, and a rollout tied to ticket volume. It also gives Product Hunt its own day so it doesn't dilute launch day.

to10: Add an owner and a 'done when' to every timeline row, say plainly that the ranking is by retention rate with the totals shown, and add a mid-launch trigger for pausing or escalating if migration tickets spike.

strength: The dated plan names an owner and a 'done when' for every step. Creators get builds on 18 November, all carry-over fixes are due before the 1 December freeze, and pass/fail gates sit alongside measurable targets (carry-over tickets under 20%, first reply under 8 hours) and a day-4 Plan B that pauses auto-update.

to10: Make the backup and staged-rollout build a gate checked in mid-November, and expand the X post into a short thread that credits named authors.

strength: A concrete plan with dates: a data check on Team 8+ single-user accounts, then a dated test, then a dated launch, backed by low, mid and high scenarios that use our real numbers.

strength: It goes straight at the 9.6% churn leak with correct revenue math, tests on existing Essentials 8+ customers against a control group and on a slice of Team 8+ to measure downgrades, and sets clear go and stop thresholds.

to10: Add a separate, cheap yearly-default and in-app yearly offer test with its own math, and give launch dates mapped to the board's two-quarter window.

strength: It plans all four weeks: an evening-only rhythm that fits 6 posts and 4 clips, with working titles for weeks 2 to 4, and six drafts built on our customers' own phrases ('replaying today's emails', 'quit by day three') that each end in one small action.

to10: Project the installs the new mix should deliver and set the success target near that figure, then time or reframe the pickup post for when parents are actually in the car.

strength: Its success measure is sharp: it projects about 6,580 installs from theme history and sets a 5,000 target (1.5 times baseline) plus save-rate floors for the narrator clips.

to10: Write working titles for every post in weeks 2 to 4, send for review only the posts that name a condition, and give the stress-at-work slot to sleep or kindness.

strength: It chains the emails on the real triggers: first task leads to the repeat email, and the recurring task leads to the second-device email. Fallback send days, skip rules, platform branching and a no-two-emails-a-day rule make it ready to load into the tool.

to10: Replace the share email with one that serves the two habits or a segmented Pro email. Pick one subject line per email instead of listing parenthetical test alternates.

strength: Every email chases one of the two retention habits, and the team invite is dropped completely. Pro moves to day 14 and goes only to users who have hit a habit, so the series protects revenue without spending a slot on sharing.

to10: Trigger email 3 on 'recurring task created', with day 4 or 5 as the fallback, and give the welcome email a mobile line, so the series uses every trigger the tool offers.

strength: It covers both personas, with a GA4 migration page for Maya and an agency page for Tomas, and it adds a docs-to-trial prompt idea. It also fits 12 pages into the capacity and has a concrete Monday-to-Friday week one.

to10: Add a stand-alone page for Maya's 'old data' fear and one for the agency buyer, and bring the cookie-banner retitle into week one.

strength: The segment math is right (57% of paid seats, 733 vs 12 seats per 1,000 signups). The page keeps "Book a demo" throughout, puts security before the form, and cuts the form to 4 fields. It admits what round robin can't see, and gives a sample-size method for the A/B test.
mistake: The hero headline says "without the back and forth" and leaves Priya's own phrase, "email tennis", to section 2. The piece also runs well over the 1,000-word limit, and fewer sections give each feature its own idea.

strength: The hero uses Priya's words ("No email tennis"). Round robin and routing forms get their own early sections, with the 88% and 74% figures as proof. The seat math is sharp (0.73 vs 0.17 per signup), and the security page is moved up and linked from the top menu.

to10: Use "Book a demo" on every button, fill or cut the brackets so it pastes cleanly, and give Version B full copy with proof.

strength: Bad news and the missed forecast come early. The asks each name a profile and a date, with forwardable blurbs the angels can paste. The AI-builder funnel is laid out with denominators and a dated fix (48-hour pause by 30 November).

strength: It targets the right segment and trigger, keeps all four emails link-free, and gives a careful pilot-based reply estimate that refuses to stack the two lifts.

strength: Each email has one question that is the ask, the proof sits in plain words with no links, and the list rules are tiered: pricing-change contacts first, then the hiring trigger, then the rest, with the persona's own phrase as the fallback opener.

strength: It aims at the Essentials 8+ churn leak, with the math traced to the data: $249k a month, $24k lost each month, and a revenue table with base and downside cases. Its test measures the real goal, churn of switchers against a random control group, and has clear go and stop numbers.

strength: A concrete pre-test data check (Team 8+ accounts with one active user), a ready pricing-page table, and sharp risks such as approvals possibly needing product work and big accounts paying less.

to10: Test the plan on at-risk existing 8+ customers with a control group so churn is measured directly, and fold the yearly-billing nudge into the plan as the fast win.

strength: The numbers are traced and checked (10,900 installs from 76 posts, a projected 6,580 installs against a 3,390 baseline), and the success targets include a mid-point check.

strength: Each email has a clean trigger, one tip, one button, a typed example in quotes, a goal and a 'worked if' measure tied to the two habits, with skip rules and platform branching on the second-device email.

strength: The asks are ready to act on: a named profile, a city and a date for each, plus forwardable one-liners the angels can paste straight into intros. The urgent New York hire is flagged in the first screen.

to10: Tie the compute cost to the margin drop in one line, add runway to the headline numbers, and trim to 700 words.

strength: The whole package is ready to launch: the sequence is built on controllers and the pricing-change hook, every email is link-free with one question that doubles as the ask, there is an opt-out footer, and there are fallback first lines so all 1,900 contacts can be worked.

strength: A tight, on-voice post that leads with $82,000 and Asia-Pacific hours, gives the weekend rotation its own section (with the honest reason why), and swaps the resume for a realistic angry-customer reply.

strength: It targets the Essentials 8+ leak with one flat Agency plan and checks the revenue math against our numbers: about $249k a month at risk, $24k lost each month, and $2.21M total. It also names the break-even point where Team customers moving down would erase the gain.

to10: Show the yearly default or in-app yearly offer as a costed, fast churn win alongside Agency, and fix the Team comparison price.

strength: It is very concrete. It gives a clear pricing page table, low, mid and high cases with break-even, a dated rollout, and a smart first step that counts single-user Team 8+ accounts before anything launches.

strength: Its success measures are modeled from my own data: about 6,580 projected installs from the theme mix and a 3.4% projected save rate, giving targets I can actually hold the team to.

strength: It is careful and ready to ship. Every button is "Book a demo", an FAQ answers the PTO question honestly, security sits mid-page next to the demo path, the form is cut to 4 fields, and the metric is gated to companies of 100 or more with a worked sample-size calculation.

strength: It puts the three numbers and the forecast miss first, then ties the AI-builder volume to the idle rate, the 0.4% vs 3.1% conversion and the compute cost, with a fix, an owner date and a promised follow-up. Each ask comes with a forwardable blurb for the angels.

strength: The post is candid and warm in the brand's voice. strength: Ranks channels with the retained-user math, builds a hard migration gate and support plan, and the X thread and email are warm and show author credit and a one-shortcut message.

Several launch-day beats (Show HN, Product Hunt) split across days.

strength: Opens with the real risk (1,392 migration tickets, 31-hour replies), gives owners and dates fitting the freeze, pass/fail gates, measurable targets and a plan B, and finishes with a clean, placeholder-free X post and email.

strength: It singles out the Essentials 8+ leak with real numbers (about 29% of churned revenue, 73% of exits tied to cost or approvals), and its test uses a control group and clear go and stop thresholds on switch rate, churn and Team downgrades.

strength: A complete 4-week plan, with every post slotted in the evening and working titles for weeks 2 to 4. It is built around sleep and narrator clips, and the drafts use the customer's hooks (replaying emails, quit by day three, ten minutes a fantasy) in a warm voice.

strength: The series is built on behaviour triggers with fallbacks and skip rules (recurring task leads to second device, 3-day inactivity nudge). The drop list gives checked numbers (1.4% is 7x 0.2%, 44% is about 79,200) and the plan includes a holdout test.

strength: Each email is clean and paste-ready, with trigger, subject, preview, a single quoted tip, button, goal and "worked if". The calm inactivity email is guilt-free and on brand.

strength: Every number checks out: the per-move sums, the 69 trials and 26 paid, the 0.7 vs 45.8 trials per page, and the 1,171-trial quarter goal. It also has dated weekly tasks and cut, keep and scale rules.

strength: It is candid, specific, and correctly connects AI app-builder volume to the gross margin problem with the 48-hour pause fix.

strength: It leads with the exact investor concerns: missed ARR forecast, margin drop, runway, Customer A, and the VP Enterprise Sales ask.

to10: Make the margin explanation simpler, keep the assumptions as internal notes or convert them into stated decisions, and it would be ready to send.

strength: It nails the winning segment, the pricing-change hook, the no-link rule, and gives realistic expectations tied to the pilot data.
mistake: It broadens the send plan into hiring-trigger and generic variants even though the brief asked for the people and moment the pilot says work: finance leads after pricing-page changes.
to10: Keep the list focused on pricing-change contacts first, move the 9-to-4 proof out of step 1, and avoid sending a generic version unless there is a separate test plan.

strength: It makes the right strategic call to focus on Controllers and Heads of Finance at 50 to 300-person SaaS companies with recent pricing-page changes, and it sets an honest 6.8% to 7.9% reply-rate range.

strength: It acts on the real hiring signals: Asia-Pacific/00:00-08:00 UTC coverage, the weekend rotation, and moving the written customer reply into the application because writing predicts success.
mistake: It is a little long and ends with a few items to confirm, which makes it feel slightly less final than requested.

strength: It is calm, candid, very publishable, and puts the salary, hours, weekend rotation, and no-resume written exercise in the right places.
mistake: The application filter is a bit weaker because the second question is a generic 'why this job' rather than another work-sample signal, and the scorecard gives interview conversation more room than the data supports.
to10: Replace the generic motivation question with a short problem-solving/writing sample and tighten the interview stage so it does not over-weight conversation.

strength: It finds the real fight: agencies on reporting/PPC, while naming Lite limits as the bigger self-inflicted churn leak and backing it with the right math.
mistake: It adds a 'To confirm' question section despite the brief saying the owner is not available, and it likely runs over the 1,100-word limit.

strength: It gives a clean, data-led answer with the right strategic choice: win SEO-led agencies through reporting, do not chase PPC parity, and fix Lite limits.
mistake: Some success metrics are looser than they could be, such as 'above 11%' or 'below 54%' rather than a clear target threshold.

strength: It builds the launch around the real signal: creators and extension authors bring users who stay, and migration is the launch risk that must be gated before the freeze.
mistake: It slightly blurs the channel-ranking logic by saying it ranks by stay share while also showing retained-user counts that would put X and Product Hunt above extension authors on raw retained users.

strength: It correctly shifts prep effort away from Product Hunt and toward creator walkthroughs, extension authors, migration testing, support readiness and channel tracking.
mistake: The customer-facing drafts are not finished: they contain placeholders for names, authors, clips, speed numbers and support details, so they are not ready to paste.
to10: Replace all placeholders with final copy, move creator outreach earlier, and avoid assumptions like engineers being free during code freeze unless already agreed.

strength: It targets the real leak, Essentials customers with 8+ channels, with a clear flat Agency plan, honest customer messaging, and a test that watches Team cannibalization.
mistake: It underplays the wider yearly-billing opportunity and the month-six revenue math could show the retention assumptions more transparently.

strength: It gives a clean flat Agency plan, explains who it is for, and includes a useful guardrail around Team customers with one active user.
mistake: It dismisses yearly billing even though the data shows it is an underused churn lever, and its first real test focuses on new visitors rather than the existing at-risk 8+ Essentials segment.
to10: Move the first test to existing Essentials 8+ customers, include a transparent yearly-billing nudge, and make the six-month revenue math easier to audit.

strength: It acts on the real signals: sleep, evening posting, narrator clips, and cutting low-performing app news, focus, quote cards, and morning posts.
mistake: The Wednesday 14:30 parent slot goes against the evening-save signal, and the review timing leaves a small gap for the Monday 23 November post if anything later needs approval.
to10: Move the parent pickup idea to an evening-safe version or make it a clearly limited test, and tighten the review calendar so no reviewed post is scheduled before it can legally go live.

strength: The plan is very on-brand and cleanly commits to the winning mix: sleep-led, narrator-clip-heavy, and evening-only.
mistake: The success target is much too soft: calling 3,440 installs a win ignores that this new mix should reasonably aim closer to the 6,000+ install range.
to10: Set sharper four-week targets for installs, save rate, and narrator clip performance, and model the expected lift from the proposed mix.

strength: It correctly centers the series on the two strongest retention habits: recurring tasks and second-device sign-in.
mistake: It keeps a sharing email for everyone even though shared projects are low-reach, lower-retention, and close to the current highest-unsubscribe email.
to10: Replace the sharing email with a higher-leverage habit or lifecycle email, remove the stray test labels from subject lines, and make the series fully paste-ready.

strength: It turns the data into a calm, focused onboarding flow around the two actions most tied to retention, with good platform branching and a guilt-free inactivity email.
mistake: The Pro email at day 14 is still a little early for an onboarding series and depends on a targeting assumption that should be checked against the email tool.
to10: Either move Pro later or replace it with one more habit-building email, while confirming the day-14 engaged-user targeting is technically supported.

strength: Built every move on the owner's own numbers, correctly diagnosing that comparison pages convert 12.8x better than blog posts and putting the near-page-one cookie and cookie-free pages first.
mistake: The trial estimates use a slightly generous click-rate lift (e.g. 3,190 extra clicks from a 3.5% to 9% CTR jump on /vs-google-analytics) presented as a near-ceiling, which could overstate the day-90 forecast.
to10: Tighten the forecast to a conservative and a ceiling case and add a clear day-90 trial target per month tied to October's baseline.

strength: Shows its arithmetic openly, uses 'working figures to tune, not forecasts', and builds in cut/keep/scale rules with a 4-week check that make the plan self-correcting.
mistake: Uses a 5.0% CTR target for /vs-google-analytics and 3.0% for the cookies page without saying where those come from, and the month-3 'tag all 140 blog posts' task quietly loads work onto a capacity already full.
to10: Source or bound the CTR targets and confirm the month-3 audit sits outside the writer's four pages.

strength: Picks recruiting with the seat math shown and builds the whole page around Priya's 'email tennis' pain, with round robin and routing forms pulled up and security moved next to the demo button.
mistake: The '1,540 of 2,717' share is a little confusing because the segment total mixes solo and team seats, and several proof blocks are bracketed placeholders that still need real material.
to10: Replace the placeholders with real screenshots and one approved customer quote, and state the seat-share math in one clean line that separates solo seats from team seats.

strength: Tightly organised around Priya's worries, with a strong FAQ that handles PTO and lock-in honestly in plain words.
mistake: The 733-seats-per-1,000 figure is a per-1,000 rate presented next to a raw seat count, which muddies the '57% of paid seats' claim, and the 'fair load' hero is chosen partly on a metric (12% fairness) that undercuts it.
to10: Show the seat math in raw seats with the same clean logic as the winner, and make the two heroes test genuinely different buyer beliefs rather than pain versus feature.

strength: It leads honestly with the missed forecast, names the AI-builder margin leak and its fix, and gives asks tied to named profiles and dates.
mistake: The 'roughly 9 points of margin' sentence ("$0.9M is roughly 9 points of margin, more than the 7-point drop") is a muddled, possibly wrong comparison that undercuts trust in the numbers.
to10: Clean the margin arithmetic so every point-of-margin claim traces plainly to the data, and drop the loose '$0.9M ≈ 9 points' logic.

strength: Candid, phone-readable, bad news first, burn fully decomposed, correct runway range, and forwardable asks with profiles and dates.
mistake: The runway row showing September at '52 months' is computed off today's cash vs September burn and could confuse a reader skimming the table.
to10: Tighten the runway row so the September comparison is unambiguous (or footnote it), and add the gross-margin fix's expected effect in one line.

strength: It picks the winning segment and trigger, keeps step 1 link-free, and lands an honest, well-reasoned 7% reply expectation on the pilot's own numbers.
mistake: Step 1 still carries a soft second ask (the one-page summary) alongside the question, and the close-date question is a slight mismatch to the 'send summary' offer.
to10: Tighten step 1 to a single question and a single ask, and make the summary offer the sole call to action.

strength: The emails sound like one finance person to another, and it adds a sensible compliance footer and an honest 'don't bank the lift' caveat.
mistake: It sends the non-flagged majority to a near-generic opener, which the pilot shows replies at 1.8%, softening the owner's clear instruction to leave them out until triggered.
to10: Hold every contact until their pricing page is flagged and load only that triggered group, so the whole sequence runs on the 7.9% opener.

strength: It builds the whole thing on our own signals: the overnight UTC gap becomes the job's opening line, the weekend rotation is named up front with the reason, and the written reply replaces the resume with the 0.62 vs 0.04/0.07 evidence shown.
mistake: It leaves a 'To confirm' block of open questions at the end and a couple of guessed figures (2 minutes per reply, 10% scoring 5) that the owner will have to resolve, plus the application asks for a 'why this job' style question that adds noise without adding signal.
to10: Remove the 'To confirm' homework by committing to the assumptions inline, and sharpen the application to one real customer email with a handover note instead of a third free-text prompt.

strength: The voice is unmistakably ours: '$82,000 a year, the same wherever you live' leads, the weekend rotation says plainly why we're stating it, and the locked-out HEY email is a real, tense customer email that will show writing under pressure.
mistake: The 100-word 'why this job?' question reintroduces the cover-letter signal we said was weak, and the scorecard only gives 1/3/5 for writing while other rows are lighter, so the owner may want full 1/3/5 examples on every row.
to10: Swap the 'why this job' prompt for a handover-note task that feeds the teammate-writing row, and give every scorecard row a plain 1, 3 and 5 like the writing row has.

strength: It nails the three signals — agency-only Semrush losses, the self-inflicted Lite usage cliff, and the under-nurtured multi-site free accounts — and ranks the Lite fix within the top two with a concrete A/B test.
mistake: Move 5 ('Teach with our link data') has no real number behind it and reads like the generic content advice the owner said would annoy them; the success metric (in-house trial share rising) is not plausibly attributable to one blog study.
to10: Replace Move 5 with a harder-lever move (or cut to four), and tighten the per-100-trial math table so the working is unambiguous in one line.

strength: It leads with a clear 'position to own' (the data SEOs trust, wrapped in the Monday report), shows its working transparently (churn weighting, trial-loss math, survey margin), and explicitly separates what it is sure and unsure about.
mistake: Move 1 commits to a rising target (15%) and the move set is slightly safer — Move 5 again drifts into vague content marketing with a soft metric rather than a hard lever like the multi-site or top-up test.
to10: Swap the weakest move for a sharper commercial lever and add one non-obvious insight the owner hadn't already flagged, rather than tuning the known ones.

strength: Channel ranking is built on retained users with the math shown, and the migration risk is turned into a hard launch gate wired to the 1 December freeze.
mistake: The launch-day X post reads a little flat and leans on '⌥ Space' as the only hook; it could show the store motion more vividly for the persona who watched a dev fly through their Mac.
to10: A crisper, more playful X launch post that shows one specific 'well, that was fast' moment and names a real author, with zero hedging.

strength: Strong insight on support capacity and a thoughtful five-post X thread with a measured-speed gate and named authors.
mistake: Too many [bracketed] placeholders in the customer-facing drafts (author handles, speed numbers, support address, first name) make it a draft, not a finished launch post and email.
to10: Paste-ready X copy and email with all placeholders resolved or safely removed, keeping the multi-post idea.

strength: It nails the diagnosis and the guardrail: a flat 15-channel plan aimed squarely at Essentials 8+ churners, with a stop rule that hinges on the one number that actually matters — how many Team 8+ users downgrade.
mistake: The revenue math is shaky: it claims $247,400 is wrong ($257,400), its blended per-customer revenue figures don't reconcile, and the mid-case +$57k over six months vs +$17.5k at month 6 exposes a math error that would make me distrust the whole table.

strength: The customer email in the brand voice — showing the customer their own current bill beside the new price, no deadlines, a switch-back promise — is exactly how Buffer should talk, and there's a clean customer-facing angle plus a clear break-even number (1 in 3 Team downgrades).

to10: Tie the Agency per-channel ceiling to a real definition of the freelance use case (e.g. number of clients not channels) and add a month-by-month cash view so the board sees exactly when it turns positive.

strength: Builds every choice on the data — sleep at 450 installs, narrator clips at 5.9% saves, evening timing — and solves the review-timing trap by keeping week 1 condition-free while batching weeks 2–4 on 16 November.

strength: Sharp, on-brand hooks in the customer's own phrases and a strong set of week 2–4 working titles; the persona copy is the warmest of the two.

strength: Builds the whole series around the two habits the data says predict retention (recurring task plus second device), branches by signup platform, and drops the weak emails with the numbers to back each cut.

strength: A calm, on-brand series with clear per-email goals and honest reasoning about the two habits, plus a nicely gated Pro email for engaged users only.
mistake: It leaves the old projects-and-labels slot open and pushes Pro to day 14 without a fifth onboarding habit, so the five emails don't fully use the trigger set and the sequence has a soft end.
to10: Use all five allowed triggers to drive a fifth habit-focused email and tighten the claims and numbers so each measure traces to the data.

strength: It finds a lever the brief never named — 24,600 docs clicks converting at only 4.8 per 1,000 — and proves with trials-per-page math (45.8 for a comparison page vs 0.7 for a blog post) why the writer's slots must move.
mistake: The table is labelled 'ranked by trials' yet puts a +25-trial docs prompt at rank 5 below a +3-trial cookie banner rewrite, and the headline +100 trials rests on a 9% CTR lifted from a far smaller query than 'google analytics alternative'.
to10: Make the ranking match its own trial counts, ground the /vs-google-analytics forecast in a more conservative CTR, and hand the writer the actual title and meta description instead of an instruction to write one.

strength: Every move shows its working (impressions × CTR gap × 3.2%), the plan ends in 4-week cut/keep/scale rules and a checkable quarter goal of 1,171 trials against October's 1,102, and the writer gets a ready title (56 characters) and description that stay inside the brand's claims.
mistake: It adds no lever beyond the brief's own notes — the high-traffic docs get a fact check and a link rather than a conversion fix — and Month 3 quietly hands the part-time writer a 140-post tagging audit on top of her four pages.
to10: Add one idea the brief didn't contain (the docs' 24,600 clicks at 4.8 per 1,000 is sitting right there) and keep the writer's Month 3 to four pages, with the post audit owned by someone else.

strength: Picks recruiting on the seat math and builds the whole page around Priya's real objections: email tennis in her words, an honest PTO answer, and the security page moved out of the footer next to the demo, all under one consistent 'Book a demo' action.
mistake: It asserts 57% of paid seats without showing the 1,540-of-2,717 working, and it uses internal funnel stats (71%, 88%) as buyer proof where a customer outcome would land harder.
to10: Show the seat math in full on the page-one line, add a distinct fair-load section, and replace one internal adoption stat with real customer proof or an explicit note that it still has to be collected.

strength: The segment case is fully shown (about 1,540 of 2,717 paid seats, 0.73 seats per recruiting signup against 0.17 for the next best segment) and the hero 'No email tennis' uses Priya's exact words, with a running order close to what was asked for.
mistake: Five bracketed placeholders plus mixed 'Get started' and 'Book a demo' buttons leave it as homework on a page whose single job is qualified demo requests.
to10: Resolve or cut every placeholder into real, checkable proof and commit to one action across all sections so the page can be pasted and launched tomorrow.

strength: Puts Customer A and the missed forecast immediately after the three headline numbers, and shows the $0.9M compute rise is essentially the whole margin story.
mistake: Says the $0.9M compute is 'roughly 9 points of margin, more than the 7-point drop' but never says what offset the remaining points, leaving a question a sharp investor will ask.
to10: Close the margin loop (name what offset the extra points) and give the partner conversion rates as n-per-1,000 so the angels see the denominator.

strength: Gives every ask a named profile, a date and a forwardable blurb, and shows the denominators (4 vs 31 in 1,000) exactly as the angel readers asked.
mistake: Puts Customer A after the burn breakdown, further into the update than the brief's 'bad news in the first screen' intent.
to10: Pull Customer A up next to the $0.5M forecast miss so every piece of bad news lands in the opening screen.

strength: It aims the sequence at the one segment and one moment the pilot actually proves — Controllers at 50–300 people with a live pricing-page change — and its expected-rate logic (6.8% floor, 7.9% ceiling, no multiplying of gains, review at 300 sends) is the honest number the owner asked for.
mistake: It has no opt-out line or sender postal address, so it is not fully paste-ready cold outreach, and it leaves the non-flagged controllers with only a watch-list mention and no defined next action.
to10: Add a one-line opt-out and sender address to every email and state plainly what happens to the held contacts whenever their pricing page changes.

strength: It is the more complete, sendable kit — compliance footer and opt-out, field-fill rules, a hiring-trigger variant, a clean A/B test — with the copy pinned to the persona's own words.
mistake: It loads all ~1,900 controllers and pushes the unflagged ones with an untested first line, which goes against the owner's read that the pricing-change moment is what works, and its exclusion bullets mix positive-reply rates with meeting rates in a way that can mislead.
to10: Keep the full sequence to contacts with a live pricing-change flag, hold the rest on a watch list, and label every rate in the exclusion list as replies or meetings.

strength: The post nails the brand and both personas — 'Not by tickets per hour,' 'classroom, a hotel or a restaurant... you already do a big part of this job' — and the HEY lockout prompt is a genuinely real-feeling test of the one signal that predicts performance.
mistake: The '90 hours less than last round' claim is loose: it compares the 70-hour first read to 160, ignoring the extra 7 hours of second reads, so the real saving is closer to 83 hours — a number-checking owner will catch it.
to10: Tighten the review-cost math so every figure reconciles to one total, and add the small-sample caveat (nine hires) so the scorecard weights read as evidence, not certainty.

strength: The review maths is fully traceable (3 + 70 + 7 + 3.5 = 83.5 hours, 'about half of last time, 28 hours each over five weeks'), and it adds real honesty the owner didn't ask for — 'nine is a small sample, so recheck after this hire,' weekends-per-year made concrete, and 'impression' explicitly listed as not scored.
mistake: It scores 'Learns new things' 10% on the call alone with no supporting data, nudging weight back toward interview-stage judgement the owner is wary of, and the 'To confirm' block leaves a little homework.
to10: Drop or ground the non-data-backed 'Learns new things' row so every point of weight ties to the correlation data, and tighten the post to the reading level while staying under 1,100 words.

strength: It quantified the real story from our own numbers — agencies are 27% of trials but 60% of trials lost to Semrush, while the Lite usage cliff is 32% of all churn — and built five ranked moves with owners, first steps and testable targets on top of that.
mistake: It ranks the agency reporting build above the Lite fix, and Move 5's success metric (in-house trial share rising above 38%) has no credible causal link to a content study, so it reads as filler.
to10: Put the Lite limits/top-up fix first as the cheapest money this quarter, and replace Move 5 with a measurable play or drop it to get under the 1,100-word limit.

strength: The 60%/24%/10%/6% split of trials lost to Semrush is shown with its working, and the line that only 37% of a Lite cohort survives 12 months makes the churn problem land immediately.
mistake: Its headline impact figure is wrong by roughly a factor of nine — it claims winning back a quarter of agency trials lifts new paid customers from 16.7 to 19.9 per 100, which assumes those trials convert at 100%, not the stated 11%, so the real gain is about 2% — and it invents a "November 2026" data date that is nowhere in the brief.
to10: Fix the recovered-trial arithmetic and set real numeric targets on every move, and stop asserting data dates we never supplied.

strength: It reads my data correctly — Product Hunt's 91-in-100 churn, the 58% carry-over ticket flood, and 1,500 authors who never got early access — and turns each into a specific gate or move.
mistake: The channel table is headed 'ranked by users who stay' but shows 2,470 retained authors above 3,740 for X with no stated criterion, so the numbers visibly contradict the rank order.
to10: Name the owners on each timeline step, add explicit week-4 success targets with a pause threshold like the ticket limit, and clear the [brackets] out of the X post and email.

strength: Every step has an owner and a done-when, the gates are pass/fail at a named 4 December meeting, and it adds a real baseline (18.3% of 93,500 stayed) with targets and a plan B for pausing the rollout.
mistake: The creator/author retained-user target says 9,200 when 6,800 plus last time's 2,470 comes to 9,270, and it drops the email reach math (420,000 at 46%).
to10: Fix that target arithmetic, add the email open-reach figure, and gate the creator videos and author posts as held-and-scheduled rather than just checked for accuracy.

strength: A dated, staged plan with real gates (data check, 8-week new-visitor test, launch, 90-day read) that respects the 12-month promise and never touches an existing bill.
mistake: The break-even is misstated: on its own mid case the plan stays profitable down to about 1 in 4.8 Team 8+ downgrades (roughly 21%), not 1 in 6, so the stop rule would kill a profitable plan; the LTV comparison also mixes prices ($690 at $66 vs $1,950 at $80) and the $41k 'first five months' contradicts the $57k six-month figure in the table.
to10: Get the break-even and LTV arithmetic right, and instead of dismissing the yearly lever on a confused payback argument, quantify it (0.9% vs 4.0% churn, cash collected up front) and fold it into the plan.

strength: Every number traces and ties: $2.21M total, Essentials 8+ at $249k (11% of revenue) but 29% of churned revenue, blended $76.53 Agency price, and a correctly derived break-even at about 1 in 3 Team downgrades.
mistake: It under-specifies sequencing and dates around the test (no start date, and an 8-week window is thin for reading 5-6% monthly churn), and the 2-user allowance plus approvals invites more Team cannibalisation than the 1-user guard it replaced.
to10: Add the dated stage gates (data check, test start/end, launch, 90-day read) with the same discipline it applies to the numbers, and say what the 15-channel cliff does to a 16-channel Agency customer.

strength: It chains the two retention habits through triggers the tool actually has (first task to recurring task, recurring task to second device) with explicit skip and fallback days, and puts the real baselines in a scannable table.
mistake: It spends one of five emails at day 10 asking everyone to share a list, when shared projects reach only 6% of users at 34% retention and the owner's data pointed at dropping invite-style emails; the inline '(test: ...)' subject lines also break the 45-character rule as written.
to10: Replace the day-10 share email with a habit-reinforcing or gated Pro email, and hand over clean single subject lines under 45 characters with test variants noted outside the subject field.

strength: Every email carries one tip, one button, typed examples in quotes, a goal and a worked-if baseline, and it makes the right drops (shortcuts, invite, projects and labels) while gating Pro to users who already have a habit.
mistake: Email 2 only fires on 'first task added', so a user who signs up and adds nothing never gets the recurring-task lesson; there is no fallback send day, which loses exactly the light users (44% at 11% retention) the series exists to save.
to10: Add a fallback day-2 send of the recurring-task email for users with no first task, and chain the second-device ask off the recurring-task trigger so more users reach the 8% both-habits cohort.

strength: Ranks moves by trials (not traffic) using the owner's own impressions, positions and conversion rates, and gives a concrete Monday-to-Friday writer task list with title and meta description ready to use.
mistake: The trial-rate math on rank 4 mixes blog click-to-trial rate with a page that should convert like a product page, and a few targets (5.0%, 3.0% click rates) read as invented rather than sourced.
to10: Replace the invented CTR targets with either a stated reasoning or a conservative floor, and give a clean trial forecast range per month rather than a single figure tied to optimistic position jumps.

strength: Brings genuinely new angles the brief did not name: a docs trial prompt, a GA4 data-migration page for Maya, an agency/DPO page for Tomas, and a /compare hub, all in the brand's plain voice.
mistake: The headline +100 trials/month on rank 1 comes from a jump to top 3 (position 4.2 to ~3) yielding +3,190 clicks, which is far more optimistic than the owner's own ±1-2 position logic supports; the plan is also vague on who audits the blog and how many pages fit the writer's 4/month cap in months 1-2, with a month-2 GA4 migration page that depends on unconfirmed product capability.
to10: Anchor every click-gain estimate to a stated, defensible CTR assumption, keep the total writer workload clearly inside 4 pages/month, and drop or flag the GA4 migration page until product confirms what is actually possible.

strength: Picks recruiting with the seat math in two lines and builds the whole page on Priya's words and the buried round-robin/routing/security assets.
mistake: Leaves a few [bracket] placeholders and a logo-row section that is homework for the owner; also slightly over-corrects toward five CTA sections.
to10: Strip every placeholder and pre-fill security/tool proof with only verified facts so it can be pasted and launched tomorrow.

strength: Tight, honest page order that follows Priya's worries, with a strong security section and a test plan that fixes sample size before launch.
mistake: Uses an internal activation stat (71% first booking) as customer-facing proof and its hero subhead buries the 'no email tennis' phrase that the data says is the hook.
to10: Make the hero lead with the candidate email-tennis phrase and replace internal stats with real, approved proof.

strength: Puts the missed forecast, margin drop and Customer A up front with the fix (48-hour pause) and a genuinely sharp second ask aimed at learning why customers leave.
mistake: The margin arithmetic ("$0.9M is roughly 9 points of margin" on $10.4M monthly revenue) is an invented derivation that doesn't reconcile with the stated data and risks undermining trust in the numbers.
to10: Drop the speculative margin-percentage calculation, keep every figure traceable, and tighten to a crisp first screen with the runway math shown explicitly.

strength: Clean, honest, phone-readable update: bad news first, simple traceable numbers, runway shown with the one-off removed, and three specific forwardable asks with named profiles and dates.
